transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Well, it's... it's a bit of a long story, but I guess the main reason I finally made the appointment is because things at work are just getting incredibly frustrating. I'm an artist, and I also do a lot of freelance design and commission work, so communication is a huge part of my day-to-day. I have my degree in this, so I'm very used to talking about my process, but lately, whenever I sit down to write my artist statements, or even just when I'm typing up basic client notes for a project, everything just gets completely tangled up. Like, I'll be in a meeting with a client or a gallery manager, and I'll start out trying to explain the tactile qualities of a piece—you know, the physical textures, the way the light hits the impasto—but then my brain just sort of skips a track, and suddenly I'm talking about the materials budget, and from there I just jump right into how the cost of the pigments actually ties into this deeper, secret meaning about societal decay and hidden energy grids. And the thing is, it all makes perfect sense to me in the moment, all the connections are so vivid and obvious, but people keep stopping me. They keep telling me they have absolutely no idea what I'm trying to explain and that they can't follow my train of thought at all. It's happening constantly, and they just stare at me like I'm speaking a completely different language, which just makes me try to explain it more, but it never helps.
Over the past few weeks, have you noticed your mood being unusually elevated, more energetic than normal, or that you need much less sleep than usual?

Well, yes, actually. I mean, it's funny you ask that because it's been happening in these really intense stretches. Like, for days at a time, I'll wake up and I just feel completely lit up from the inside. It's this buzzing, unstoppable feeling, and I'll be in my studio at, like, 3:00 AM, mixing colors, and every single idea I have feels absolutely brilliant. Like I'm finally tapping into the real frequency of the universe, you know? The energy is just pouring out of me, and I don't even feel tired. I'll just keep working and working. But the problem is, it's not always this happy, productive thing. Because when I'm in that zone, and I'm feeling so connected and electric, if a collaborator or a client says even one tiny thing—like, maybe they just question a color choice or ask a completely innocent question about a deadline—I just snap. And I mean, I really snap. It's like this sudden, explosive irritation that bubbles up out of nowhere, and I get so defensive and angry in a way that I know, somewhere in the back of my mind, is totally out of proportion to what they actually said. It feels so much bigger than the situation, but in that second, I just can't tolerate anyone interrupting my flow or questioning the brilliance of what I'm doing. So it's this weird mix of feeling like a genius who doesn't need sleep, but also feeling like a live wire that's going to shock anyone who gets too close.

Do these intense feelings of special insight or connections—like the ideas about hidden meanings and energy grids—ever occur even when you're not in one of these high-energy, sleepless stretches, such as during times when your mood feels normal?

Yeah, actually, they do. And that's what's so confusing to me, because you'd think it would only happen when I'm all wired up, right? But I remember, maybe a couple of months ago, there was this whole period—probably a solid four weeks, maybe a little longer—where I felt totally fine. I mean, my mood was completely flat, normal, whatever you want to call it. I was sleeping my usual seven or eight hours, I was waking up at a reasonable time, drinking my coffee, going to the studio... I wasn't buzzing, I wasn't staying up all night, I wasn't snapping at people. It was just a really quiet, average month. 

But even then, even when I was feeling totally level, the weird stuff was still happening. Like, I'd be in the studio, just quietly organizing my supplies, and I would hear these... comments. Just these whispering, critical comments coming from right behind the shelving units where I keep my canvases. It wasn't like a booming voice, just this persistent muttering about what I was doing. And it wasn't just the voices, either. I would be looking at my ordinary materials—like a jar of gesso or a tube of cadmium red—and I would just *know* there were hidden warnings in them. Like the way the label was printed or the exact placement of the barcode was trying to communicate this urgent, secret message to me about the energy grids. I spent hours trying to decode the warnings on the back of a canvas stretcher once. And again, I wasn't manic or energetic at all. I was just sitting there, feeling completely normal in my body, but my brain was still picking up on all these hidden signals and hearing those comments from behind the shelves. It lasted for weeks like that, just this quiet, steady stream of... of secrets, I guess, right in the middle of a totally normal month.

Over the entire time you've been experiencing these symptoms, roughly how long in total have you had psychotic experiences—like the whispering voices or hidden messages—compared to how long you've had the manic or mood episodes?

Well, gosh, if I'm really looking back over the whole timeline of everything... I mean, I've been keeping track in my head, obviously, because it all affects my studio schedule and my client meetings so much. If I had to weigh it all out, the energized, irritable, overproductive stretches—you know, the times when I'm up all night and my brain is just firing on all cylinders and I'm snapping at people—those have definitely taken up more of the year overall. It's like, even though the intensity of that electric feeling rises and falls, and sometimes it's this absolute peak of frantic energy and other times it's just this simmering, agitated hum where I'm working fast but not completely flying... those periods just dominate the calendar. 

The calmer stretches, like that quiet month I told you about where my mood was flat but I was still hearing the whispering and seeing the warnings... those definitely happen, and they last for weeks at a time, which is so strange to experience. But if you put them side by side, the high-energy, irritable phases are just a much bigger chunk of the picture. It's almost like the quiet periods are just these little valleys between these massive, sprawling mountains of energy, if that makes sense. And even when I'm in the valleys, the weird stuff is still there, but the mountains just take up so much more space on the map. I was actually looking at my planner the other day, trying to color-code when I felt which way, because as an artist, visual data really helps me process things, and I noticed that the pages are just covered in the markers I use for those wired, sleepless times...

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes concurrent manic episodes (elevated/irritable mood, decreased need for sleep, increased energy, grandiosity, disorganized/tangential speech) together with psychotic features (auditory hallucinations of whispering voices, delusions of hidden messages in labels/materials). Critically, the patient also reports a distinct ~4-week period of euthymic mood during which the hallucinations and delusions persisted in the absence of any mood symptoms, satisfying the requirement for psychotic symptoms occurring for at least 2 weeks without a mood episode. However, when reviewing the total course of illness, mood episodes (manic phases) have been present for the majority of the total duration of the illness, distinguishing this from schizophrenia with mood symptoms. This combination—mood episodes for the majority of the illness plus psychotic symptoms independent of mood episodes for a significant duration—meets criteria for schizoaffective disorder, bipolar type (F25.0), rather than bipolar disorder with psychotic features (F31.2) or schizophrenia (F20.9).
